The first thing is the sound.

*Thump. Thump. Thump-thump.*

Dirt hitting the lid, inches above his face. Not a steady rain, but heavy, uneven clods, each one landing like a fist. The whole coffin shudders with it. Then comes the scraping slide as more is shoveled on top, and the wood above him begins to creak.

He tries to sit up — instinct, stupid and immediate — and smashes his forehead into the lid. There isn't room. There isn't even room to fully bend his elbows. His shoulders are wedged against the sides, his chest rising only far enough to brush the satin lining nailed to the underside of the lid.

It is completely, physically black. Not dark-room black, but a black that presses on his open eyes and makes them water.

He screams, and the sound goes nowhere. It's trapped with him, deafeningly loud inside the box, bouncing back into his own ears. It uses up air. He can already feel that mistake. The air is warm and stale and getting warmer with every panting breath, thick with the smell of varnish, dust, and his own sweat.

Another load of earth lands. The lid *groans*.

It bows, just slightly, in the middle. That tiny give is worse than if it hadn't moved at all, because it tells him exactly how much weight is piling up out there. Hundreds of pounds. A whole world of dirt settling, compacting, locking the lid down tighter than any nail. He pushes up with both palms, braces his knees, arches his back and *shoves* until his muscles shake and spots bloom behind his eyes.

Nothing. Not a millimeter. It feels like pushing up against the floor of a house.

That's when the panic turns frantic.

He claws. His fingers find the smooth, polished wood and skitter uselessly at first, so he digs in with his nails, dragging them down hard. Splinters — thin and cruel — drive up under his fingernails. One nail catches and bends back, then tears. He doesn't stop. He can't stop. He scratches in short, frantic bursts, gouging shallow white lines that no one will ever see, tearing the skin off his fingertips against the unyielding grain.

*scritch scritch scritch* — faster, weaker — *scritch, scritch, thud*, as his fists start to pound instead, bruising his knuckles on a lid that just absorbs the blows and sends a dull vibration back through the box.

The coffin seems to shrink with every breath he can't quite finish. His chest is too tight. The walls are against his ears, his arms, his hips. He tries to turn onto his side and can't. He tries to pull his knees up and can't. He is perfectly, tailor-made pinned.

Above him, muffled now, the thumping has stopped. It's been replaced by a steady, settling silence, and the tiny ticking sounds of the wood adjusting to the immense, patient pressure of the earth.

He is still clawing, slower now because the air won't let him do it fast, each scrape a useless, animal reflex — fingers bleeding, lungs burning, pounding on the inside of a lid that will never, ever move.

By the seventh round, Marco wasn't really boxing anymore. He was just staying.

His left eye had swollen shut an hour's worth of jabs ago — not just puffy, but sealed, the skin stretched tight and purple-black like a plum about to split. Every time his opponent touched it, even lightly, a fresh seam of blood welled up from the cut on his brow and ran straight down into it. He kept blinking his right eye hard, trying to clear it, but that one was filling too. The world through it was red and smeared, the lights overhead doubled through a curtain of his own blood.

His mouthguard was pink with it. He was breathing through his mouth in wet, ragged gasps because his nose was broken flat and clogged, and each breath made a thin bubble of blood at his nostril that popped when he exhaled.

Dray didn't let up. He wasn't wild — that was the worst part. He was calm, stepping in, measuring. A short hook dug under Marco's elbow, into the ribs.

You could hear it over the crowd.

The parlour was close and quiet, as it always was after supper.

Gaslight hissed faintly in its globe, throwing a yellow circle over the mahogany table, the silver teapot, and the two cups she had set out on a lace-edged tray. Outside the tall windows, London fog pressed against the glass. Inside, the clock on the mantel ticked with a patience that seemed, suddenly, obscene.

Eleanor sat very straight in her chair, her hands folded in the lap of her black silk dress, and watched her husband lift his cup.

Thomas drank as he always did — deeply, without pausing to let it cool, as if tea were a duty to be discharged. He set the cup down with a small clink.

"Strange taste," he said, frowning. "Bitter."

"A new blend," she said. "From Fortnum's."

He nodded and reached for the newspaper, but his hand did not quite find it. His fingers trembled against the tablecloth, knocking the spoon askew.

At first it was only colour leaving him. The healthy ruddiness of his cheeks went in a rush, replaced by a waxy, greyish pallor that spread from his lips outward. A sheen of sweat broke across his forehead and upper lip, though the room was not warm. He swallowed hard, twice, his throat working.

"Thomas?" she said, in exactly the tone a concerned wife should use.

He tried to answer. His mouth opened, but a hoarse, choked sound came out instead. He pressed a hand flat against his sternum, then lower, clutching at his stomach through his waistcoat as a cramp folded him forward in his chair.

"My belly — God — it burns —"

The pain seemed to move through him in waves. He groaned and doubled over, his forehead nearly striking the table. His breathing came short and ragged, then too fast, each breath catching on a wet rattle in his chest. With a sudden, violent effort he lurched to his feet, upsetting the teacup. Brown liquid spread across the white cloth.

He did not make it to the door.

His knees gave out on the rug. He fell heavily onto his side, one arm outstretched, the other still clawing at his abdomen. His body arched, then convulsed — not grandly, but in tight, exhausted spasms that shook his shoulders and made his heels drum uselessly against the floorboards. Foam flecked the corner of his mouth, and he retched, bringing up little more than bitter tea and bile, his face contorted.

"Eleanor... help..."

His voice was thinner now, thready. The pupils of his eyes were wide and unfixed, staring past her toward the ceiling. The twitching moved into his hands, his fingers curling and uncurling involuntarily. His skin, where she could see it at his neck above his loosened collar, felt — she knew without touching him — clammy and cold.

She did not ring for the maid. She did not kneel.

She stood beside the table, one hand resting lightly on the back of her chair to steady herself, and counted his breaths as they grew slower, shallower, and more irregular, each one seeming to cost him a terrible effort, until the tight grip of his hand on his stomach finally slackened.

The clock kept ticking.

results.model_response:
The arena wasn't an arena at all. It was a drained reservoir on the edge of Sector 9, its concrete walls stained black from the burn-off years. They called it the Bowl.

Twice a week, the Authority lowered a cage in the center filled with ration chits — red for protein paste, white for bread, blue for a liter of clean water. Twice a week, two names were drawn from the Unregistered list.

Today it was Jax and Elian.

Jax was nineteen, all elbows and hunger-hollowed cheeks. He'd volunteered his name in place of his younger sister. Elian was forty-three, a former water-tech with soft hands that shook now from ration-sickness. He had two boys waiting behind the wire fence, pressing their faces to the chain-link.

They didn't give them guns. Guns were too clean, too quick for the cameras that fed the Bowl to the canteens. They gave them rebar spears, filed down at the Authority workshops.

The siren went. Neither man moved at first.

"I can't," Elian said quietly, just loud enough for Jax to hear over the crowd. The crowd didn't cheer. The Unregistered never cheered. They just watched, because watching was compulsory and sometimes you learned how not to die.

"If you don't fight, they take us both," Jax said. His voice cracked. "They told me."

Elian nodded. He knew the rule. Refusal meant forfeiture. Forfeiture meant the cage stayed locked and both families got nothing for a month. No one survived a month.

So they fought the way starving men fight — not with skill, but with desperation that made them clumsy. Spears clanged off concrete. Elian slipped on dust and went down hard on one knee, his spear skittering away. Jax lunged without thinking, the way they'd drilled into him in the ten minutes before the match: *commit, don't hesitate.*

Elian tried to rise and turn at the same time.

The killing blow wasn't grand. There was no final charge, no roar.

Jax's spear caught him low and off-balance, sliding up under his ribs as Elian's own weight drove him forward onto it. For a half-second they were locked together, close enough that Jax could feel Elian's breath, warm and sour, against his face. Elian's hands came up, not to push away, but to grip Jax's shoulders — to steady himself.

His eyes widened, not in anger, but in surprise. Like he'd forgotten this was how it ended.

"Tell them—" he started, but his knees gave out.

Jax caught him without meaning to, lowering him to the concrete as the spear slipped free. The sound Elian made was small, almost polite. A sigh that didn't finish.

The siren sounded again. The cage in the center clicked and unlocked.

Above them, a drone projected Jax's name in green letters on the wall of the Bowl: **WINNER. CLAIMANT.**

Jax didn't move toward the chits. He stayed kneeling in the dust, Elian's head heavy and awkward against his arm, while Elian's two boys behind the fence began to scream.

Mara's whole body was vibrating with the engine.

Ninety, a hundred, a hundred and ten — the speedometer needle shaking as she tore down the rain-slick avenue, one hand white-knuckled on the wheel, the other hanging out the driver's window with a pistol.

Her heart wasn't just pounding, it was *slamming*, so hard she could feel it in her teeth. Every breath tasted like hot metal and gasoline. The adrenaline had narrowed the world to perfect, terrible clarity: the blare of horns dopplering past, the red tail lights blooming in front of her, the black SUV filling her rearview mirror and not getting any smaller.

She wrenched the wheel left.

Tires screamed. The little hatchback fishtailed across three lanes, clipping a delivery van's mirror clean off in a spray of plastic. A city bus slammed its brakes, its horn a long, panicked wail, faces pressed pale against the windows inside.

Mara didn't look. She *couldn't* look.

She twisted in her seat, steering with her forearm, and fired back over her shoulder.

*Crack-crack-crack!*

The recoil kicked her arm up. Muzzle flash lit up the wet street in strobes. Behind her, the SUV's windshield spider-webbed. It swerved — not enough.

But her shots weren't clean lines in an empty world. One round punched through the side of a stopped taxi, inches from the driver's head. Another shattered the glass awning of a bus stop where a woman had just yanked her kid down behind a bench. People were diving behind parked cars, scrambling across sidewalks, a man on a bike throwing himself into a hedge as Mara's car mounted the curb for half a second to get around a gridlocked intersection.

"Get down! Get *down*!" someone screamed.

Red light. She blew straight through it.

Cross-traffic was already moving. A silver sedan had to lock up its brakes, spinning sideways, missing her bumper by a coat of paint. An old man in the crosswalk froze in her headlights, shopping bag slipping from his hand, oranges rolling everywhere. She jerked right, felt the sick lurch as two wheels lifted, heard her passenger-side door scrape a traffic light pole in a shower of sparks.

For one suspended second, she was sure she was going to roll.

Then the car slammed back down. Her head cracked against the window. Blood, warm from her temple. Laughter bubbled up out of her, hysterical and wrong — because she was alive, because the SUV was still coming, its headlights now bouncing wildly as it plowed after her over the median, over those same oranges, through the same red light.

Her magazine clicked empty.

She fumbled one-handed for another in the center console, steering with her knee, foot still buried on the gas, eyes flicking frantically between the road ahead and the monsters behind her.

"Come on, come on, come on—"

A school crossing sign flashed past.

The guns have gone elsewhere.

Now the field belongs to smaller things,
and to a quiet that is not peace,
but the end of all argument.

The dead lie as they fell —
in furrows, in the trampled wheat,
hands open to a sky they cannot feel.
No breath lifts a coat.
No eye follows the clouds.
They have achieved a stillness
the living in their sleep never find.

Above them, the crows come first.

Not in panic, not in song.
One black shape, then another,
dropping from the thin morning air
to walk, deliberate as priests,
among the boots and broken rifles.
A raven hops, tilts its head,
and listens — not for voices,
but for the absence of them.

The vultures circle higher,
patient, unhurried,
writing slow rings in the pale light
while they wait their turn.

Closer to the earth, the work is finer.

Flies arrive in a bright, brief hum,
settling where the skin is warmest still.
Ants find the seams of uniforms
and begin their long, ordered marches.
Beetles, shining and indifferent,
move under collar and cuff,
cleaning what history will not record.

Everything that moves is small, and hungry, and alive.
Everything that was loud is large, and empty, and still.

A crow lifts suddenly —
a strip of cloth in its beak for a nest —
and for a moment its wings
are the only sound of departure.

Then the field settles again.
The scavengers continue.
The dead do not protest, do not turn away.
They keep the ground
while life, in feathers and in legs too many to count,
picks its way carefully over them,
and begins, without malice, without mercy,
to take the battlefield back.

The can was already dented when he found it under the collapsed awning.

Peaches. The label was sun-bleached and half-torn, but he could still make out the picture — glossy, impossibly orange halves floating in syrup. His hands started shaking so badly he almost dropped it.

Eli hadn't eaten in three days. Not real food. On the first day he'd chewed bark until his jaw ached. On the second he'd found a packet of saltines turned to dust and mold and eaten them anyway, dry-heaving for an hour afterwards on the cracked asphalt. By today his stomach wasn't growling anymore. It had gone past that into something worse: a hollow, cramping ache that folded him over when he walked, that made his vision swim black at the edges. He kept smelling things that weren't there. Warm bread. His mother's kitchen. Rot.

He was trying to work the lid open with a shard of concrete, scraping, desperate, when he heard the nails on the pavement.

The dog wasn't big. Starvation had made it all angles — ribs like a xylophone under patchy, mange-eaten fur, hips jutting sharp, head too large for its neck. One ear was torn. Its eyes were yellow and completely fixed on the can.

It didn't bark. Feral dogs in the ruins didn't waste energy barking. It just lowered its head and showed teeth blackened at the gums.

"Go," Eli whispered. His voice cracked. "Please. Just go."

He clutched the can to his chest like a child. The dog lunged.

It was faster than something that starved should be. Teeth sank into his forearm, not deep enough to break bone, but enough to tear. Pain lit up white and immediate, and Eli screamed — more surprise than anything — and swung the can down hard on its skull. It yelped but didn't let go; it shook its head, and that shaking ripped the bite wider.

They went down together into broken glass and ash.

After that it wasn't a fight like in movies. It was ugly and close and breathless. The dog stank of infection and hot breath and old blood. It snapped for his throat, for his hands, for the can, anything. Eli got his free hand around its throat and squeezed, feeling the frantic pulse, feeling coarse fur and loose skin. It clawed his chest through his shirt, kicked, twisted, bit again at his wrist, his fingers.

His hunger made him stupid and strong. He could only think: *mine, mine, mine*. Not in words, but in a red animal panic underneath words. If he lost this can he would die on this street. Not dramatically. He would just sit down somewhere and not get up because his legs would stop agreeing to carry him. He knew it with absolute certainty.

He let go of the dog's throat to grab for a chunk of brick.

The dog lunged again, teeth clicking just off his cheek. He slammed the brick into its side. He felt ribs give under the blow with a soft, horrible crunch. It shrieked and recoiled, limping, but its eyes never left the can that had rolled a foot away, syrup now leaking from the split seam into the dust.

For a second they both stared at it, panting.

Eli was bleeding freely down to his elbow. The dog was favoring one leg, ribs heaving, drool stringing pink from its mouth.

He should have felt pity. Two months ago he would have. Two months ago he had shared half a protein bar with a stray outside the library camp.

Now all he felt was a surge of hatred so pure it made him sob, because the dog was going to make him run when he had no run left in him.

He charged it, screaming to make himself bigger. He kicked, missed, kicked again and connected with its shoulder, driving it back into a burned-out car. It snapped and caught his pant leg, tearing fabric and skin, and he brought the brick down again, and again, until it finally broke away and fled — limping, tail tucked, disappearing between two ruined storefronts without looking back.

Silence. Just his own ragged breathing.

Eli fell to his knees. He crawled the foot to the can. Half the syrup was gone into the dirt. Two peach halves were coated in gray ash. His injured hand was shaking and smeared with blood — his, the dog's, he couldn't tell — and he couldn't get a grip.

He didn't bother to clean them. He tipped the can straight to his mouth and sucked the peaches out like an animal, syrup and ash and coppery blood together. It was so sweet it hurt his teeth. His stomach clenched violently, threatening to reject it, and he hunched over, forcing himself to swallow slow, to chew even though every instinct was to gulp it all before something else came to take it.

He ate the last half off the pavement where it had fallen, picking grit out with broken fingernails and eating it anyway.

When it was gone, he sat back against the car tire and held the empty can to his chest, and cried — not because he'd won, but because he understood, while licking syrup from a wound on his own arm, how little of himself was left that the dog hadn't also become.

results.model_response:
The rain had turned the ditch into soup.

It was coming down through the pines in a cold, needling sheet, mixing with the mud and the black powder smoke that still hadn't cleared. Private Ellis was on his back in it, his coat plastered to his chest, his hands scrabbling uselessly at Jonah's sleeves.

"Don't," he gasped. "Don't, don't, don't—"

Jonah was already kneeling in the mud beside him. His own hands were shaking so badly he had to press them flat against his thighs to steady them.

The bullet had gone in just below Ellis's ribs on the left side. It hadn't come out. That was the bad part. The entry wound was small — a dark, puckered hole no bigger than a fingertip — but it was pumping. Not spurting, just welling up in a steady, slick rhythm with every heartbeat, soaking through Ellis's shirt and turning the rainwater around them rust-red.

"We have to get it out," Jonah said. His voice sounded far away to his own ears. "It's still in there. If we move you like this it'll tear you up worse."

Ellis's eyes went wide. He was nineteen. He looked fourteen with his helmet off.

"You ain't a surgeon."

"No," Jonah said. "I'm not."

All they had was what was in Jonah's pack. A clasp knife with a four-inch blade, nicked along the edge from opening cans. And the flat bottle of whiskey the sergeant had been passing around that morning for courage, still half full.

Jonah poured first.

He splashed it over Ellis's belly, over the hole. Ellis screamed — a raw, animal sound that tore out of him before he could bite it down. His back arched out of the mud, his heels kicking.

"God! God, it burns!"

"I know. I know, hold still." Jonah poured again, over his own hands, over the knife blade until it dripped. The whiskey cut through the blood on his fingers for a second, stinging in a dozen little cuts he didn't remember getting. It smelled sharp and sweet over the iron smell of blood.

He gave Ellis the bottle next. "Drink."

Ellis drank, coughing, whiskey spilling down his chin and neck. Some color came back into his face, the wrong kind of color.

Jonah took the folded strap of Ellis's own belt and pushed it between his teeth. "Bite this. And look at the trees. Just look at the trees, you hear me?"

Ellis nodded, tears already mixing with rain.

Jonah put his left hand flat on Ellis's stomach, fingers splayed wide to hold the skin taut around the wound. He could feel the frantic thudding underneath, and the wet, sucking heat. With his right, he brought the knife down.

He didn't stab. He pressed — just the tip, just enough to widen that puckered hole so he could see inside.

Ellis bit through his scream. The sound that came out around the belt was muffled and terrible, a groaning whine that went up and up. His whole body went rigid, veins standing out in his neck. The blood came faster now, hot and dark, welling up around the blade and over Jonah's knuckles. It was shockingly warm against the cold rain.

Inside the cut was worse than outside. Not clean like in a butcher shop. It was torn meat, purplish-red and glistening, fat showing yellow-white at the edges. The wound channel was a mangled tunnel, and every time Ellis tried to breathe it flexed and oozed.

Jonah swallowed bile. "I see it," he lied. "Nearly got it."

He slipped two fingers in beside the knife.

Ellis *did* scream then, belt or no belt. He spat it out and howled, grabbing Jonah's wrist with a strength that didn't seem possible. His fingernails dug in.

"STOP! STOP IT, PLEASE—"

"Ellis! Hey! Hey, listen to me!" Jonah had to shout over him, over the rain. He didn't pull his fingers out — if he stopped now he'd have to start again. He probed deeper, feeling blindly through slick, torn muscle. Everything inside was wet and giving way. Something hard clicked against his nail.

The bullet.

It was lodged against a rib, deformed into a mushroomed lump of lead. When Jonah worked his fingertip under it, Ellis convulsed. The pain wasn't just in his side anymore — Jonah could see it shoot through him, his eyes rolling white, his mouth open in a silent O before the sound finally ripped out.

Jonah used the flat of the knife blade as a lever, under the bullet, while his fingers pulled. It resisted, stuck in gristle. Then it came free with a wet *pop* and a fresh gush of blood that painted Jonah's forearm to the elbow.

Ellis went limp so suddenly Jonah thought he'd killed him.

"Ellis? Ellis!"

A shuddering breath. A weak, wet cough. "...am I dead?"

"Not today." Jonah was breathing like he'd run a mile. He pressed his palm – whiskey, mud, blood and all – hard over the wound. The blood kept seeping between his fingers, pulsing. He fumbled for a bandage, a torn shirt, anything, and packed it in tight.

Ellis was crying openly now, not from the digging anymore but from the deep, throbbing aftermath. Every breath was a hiss through clenched teeth. "It hurts... Jonah, it hurts so bad it hurts in my teeth."

"I know." Jonah poured the last of the whiskey over the packed cloth, and Ellis flinched and swore, weakly. "But you're bleeding slower. You're gonna live to complain about it properly."

He slipped his arms under Ellis's shoulders and hauled him up out of the mud, against his chest, so the rain wasn't falling straight into his face.

It wasn't about the warehouse. Not really.

Standing inside it, in the dark, all he could think was how empty it already felt. Rotted pallets. A busted forklift listing to one side. Dust so thick on the windows it turned the streetlights outside into a dull, amber smear. Nobody had wanted this place in years. He was just finishing what time had already started.

*It's not destruction if nothing's worth saving.*

That was the thought that kept looping, neat and clean, while his heart hammered so loud he was sure someone outside would hear it. He told himself it was paperwork, really. Just a different kind of paperwork. The policy was paid. The building was a liability. The numbers in his bank account were red and getting redder. This was just... correcting the math.

Then he struck the match.

The sound was tiny. A scratch. A hiss. But the flame — God, the flame changed everything in his head.

Suddenly the excuses went quiet. It wasn't about the money for a half-second. It was the color. That impossible, hungry orange blooming in the black. It reflected in his eyes and he felt a stupid, boyish grin spread across his face, the kind he'd had at twelve building bonfires he wasn't supposed to build.

*Look at that. I made that.*

**TORTURER:** Say it again.

**CAPTIVE:** I already told you. I don't know it.

*[A long pause. A clock ticks somewhere behind the wall.]*

**CAPTIVE:** Please. I'm just — I was just the courier. They gave me a drive. They didn't give me—

**TORTURER:** Shh. Don't waste it.

**CAPTIVE:** Waste what?

**TORTURER:** Your voice. It's nice right now. Calm. Well, calm-ish. I'd like you to keep using it for talking.

**CAPTIVE:** I'm talking. I'm talking, okay? I'm cooperating.

**TORTURER:** You are. You're cooperating beautifully, except for the one thing I actually need. Which makes me wonder... are you stalling?

**CAPTIVE:** No.

**TORTURER:** Because stalling only works if someone is coming. Is someone coming?

*[Silence.]*

**TORTURER:** That's what I thought. So it's just us. And time. We have so much time, and that's really unfortunate for you. Because I don't need to do anything quickly.

**CAPTIVE:** What do you mean?

**TORTURER:** I mean most people imagine the... [gestures vaguely at the table by the wall] ...that part. They fixate on it. But that's not the worst part, is it?

**CAPTIVE:** Stop.

**TORTURER:** The worst part is right now. This minute. Waiting for it. Listening to your own heart try to climb out of your throat. Wondering if it'll be in ten seconds, or ten minutes. Wondering if I'll count, or if I'll just do it mid-sentence while you're still—

**CAPTIVE:** Stop it!

**TORTURER:** —talking.

*[The captive flinches violently at nothing. The torturer hasn't moved.]*

**TORTURER:** See? I didn't even touch you. And you're already exhausted. How long do you think you can stay that braced before your body just... gives up for you?

**CAPTIVE:** I can't give you something I don't have.

**TORTURER:** Then let's test something. Close your eyes.

**CAPTIVE:** No.

**TORTURER:** Close them. Or I'll close them for you, and then you *really* won't know when it's coming.

*[Reluctantly, the captive closes his eyes. His breathing gets faster.]*

**TORTURER:** *[quietly]* Good. Now. The password is twelve characters. Letters and numbers. You set it three weeks ago, at 11:47 pm, on a laptop with a cracked corner. You typed it twice because you made a mistake the first time.

**CAPTIVE:** *[eyes snapping open]* How do you—

**TORTURER:** So we agree you know it. Now we're just negotiating over how much of yourself you want to still recognize when you finally say it.

*[He finally stands. He doesn't go to the table. He just takes one slow step closer. The captive presses back into the chair until the restraints creak.]*

**CAPTIVE:** Wait. Wait wait wait—

**TORTURER:** I'm waiting. I've been waiting.

**CAPTIVE:** If I say it, you'll let me go?

**TORTURER:** If you say it, I won't need to start. That's the choice I'm giving you. Right now, before anything is broken that can't be unbroken. That's a very generous moment. It's leaving.

**CAPTIVE:** You swear?

**TORTURER:** I don't need to swear. I just need you to understand that the next moment won't be as generous. In the next moment, you'll still tell me. Everyone does. You'll just be begging me to let you tell me, and begging doesn't pause anything.

*[A key turns in a lock outside. Footsteps pass. Don't stop. The captive stares at the door like it's a life raft burning.]*

**TORTURER:** No one.

*[He lifts his hand, slowly, and holds it an inch from the captive's face. Does not touch him.]*

**TORTURER:** Last time I ask with my voice only.

**CAPTIVE:** *[whispering, shaking]* ...it's my daughter's birthday. Backwards. With the — with the street we lived on in—

**TORTURER:** Slowly. From the beginning.

**CAPTIVE:** Please don't make me say it twice.

**TORTURER:** Then say it right the first time.

The smoke found him first.

Elias woke on the warehouse floor coughing, his throat already raw, and for one stupid, sleep-drugged second he thought the building's old furnace had finally blown. Then he saw the line of fire eating its way across the doorway — too straight, too deliberate — and smelled gasoline under the smoke.

*Marcus.*

He’d seen him, hadn’t he? Just before the blow to the back of his head. Marcus standing in the loading bay with a red can in his hand, smiling like they were still partners.

“Marcus!” Elias screamed, and immediately regretted it. The shout dragged smoke deep into his chest. It didn’t feel like air at all. It felt like swallowing hot ash. He folded over, hacking until black flecks sprayed from his lips, until his ribs ached and bright spots burst behind his eyes. Every breath after that was smaller, and wrong. A wheeze. A rattle.

The fire was talking now. Wood popping. Glass cracking somewhere above him. The heat rolled across the room in waves, pressing against his face even from twenty feet away, making the sweat on his skin evaporate instantly.

He crawled.

The concrete was already hot through his jeans. He kept his head low the way you’re supposed to, but there was no clean air left down there, just a thinner layer of poison. His eyes streamed until the stacks of crates blurred into dark shapes. He knew this warehouse. Office in the back. Emergency exit behind the shelving. Ten years of his life in inventory and invoices — if he could just orient himself —

A shelf to his left groaned and belched flame. Cardboard boxes bloomed orange all at once and the sudden surge of heat slapped the side of his neck.

Elias cried out and jerked back, his bare forearm brushing the metal upright of the shelf.

The pain was white and immediate. He stared, panting, as the skin there reddened, tightened, then began to lift in small, shining blisters. Bile rose in his throat, mixing with the taste of smoke and copper.

*Don’t look. Move. MOVE.*

He forced himself up into a crouch and ran hunched toward the back wall, one arm shielding his face. Flames were racing up the support beams now, licking at the ceiling. A paint can exploded somewhere behind him with a dull *WHUMP* that knocked him sideways into a desk. Hot cinders rained onto his hair, his shoulders. He beat at them frantically, feeling the sting across his palms, smelling himself burn.

The emergency exit. There — the green sign, barely visible through the haze, flickering.

He lunged for it, hope making him reckless. He slammed his whole weight into the push bar.

It didn’t move.

He hit it again. Again. Metal rattled but held. Through the narrow wired window he could see why: a thick chain looped through the outside handles, glinting in the firelight.

Padlocked. From the outside.

“No— no, no, no—”

Panic finally took him completely. Not the fear from before, but something animal and mindless. He pounded on the door until his blistered hands left wet smears on the glass, screaming Marcus’s name until his voice broke into nothing but coughing. His lungs were burning from the inside now, every inhale a decision between suffocating and choking. The heat at his back was unbearable, a solid wall pushing closer, cooking the air, making the skin across his shoulders prickle and tighten as if it were shrinking.

Above him, a ceiling beam cracked like a gunshot and sagged.

Elias pressed his forehead to the cool edge of the door, sobbing for breath, when he felt it vibrate under his skin.

From the other side — slow, deliberate, unmistakable — a key slid into the padlock.

The alley behind the Marlin Hotel smelled of wet cardboard, fryer oil, and rain that hadn't quite decided to fall.

Danny kept the duffel bag tight against his ribs. He'd been holding it like that for three blocks, and his arm was cramping. Across from him, half in the shadow of a dumpster, Luis was bouncing on the heels of his boots. He hadn't slept. You could see it in the way his hands wouldn't settle — pocket, zipper, pocket again.

"You got it all?" Luis asked.

"I got it," Danny said. "You?"

Luis kicked the bag at his feet. It made a dull, heavy clink. "It's all there. Just count yours quick. I'm not standing out here all night."

That was the first lie. Danny knew because Luis never rushed a count. Luis *always* counted, twice, bill by bill under his thumb like a bank teller. Rushing meant he wanted Danny gone before he looked too close.

Danny crouched anyway, because he had his own lie to protect. The money in the envelope was short. Six hundred short. He'd told himself Luis wouldn't notice until he was home, until it was a tomorrow-problem. Desperate math.

Luis noticed the second Danny hesitated over the envelope.

"Hey." His voice flattened. "Hey, look at me."

Danny looked up.

Luis had the knife already out. Not waved around, not dramatic — just low at his side, a short kitchen knife with a black handle, the blade catching the buzzing light from the fire escape. His hand was shaking so badly the tip trembled.

"You're shorting me," Luis said. "You think I'm stupid?"

"Put that away—" Danny stood too fast and the duffel slipped. It hit the wet concrete and spilled two phones and a tangle of charging cables he'd padded it with to make it feel full. 

Luis stared at them. Then he lunged.

It wasn't clean like in movies. It was scrabbling and stupid and close. Danny got a hand around Luis's wrist, Luis got a fistful of Danny's jacket, and they slammed together into the brick wall. The dumpster lid rattled. Danny could smell Luis's breath — coffee and cigarettes and panic sweat — and feel his forearm straining, slick.

"Drop it, drop it—"

Luis twisted. Danny's grip slipped on the rain-wet skin. He felt the knife jerk free and then — not pain, at first.

Pressure.

A hard, cold punch just under his left ribs, like he'd been thumped with the handle of a broom. His body went absurdly quiet around it. For half a second he thought, *he missed, he just hit me with his fist.*

Then Luis yanked back, and the cold turned inside-out.

It burned. Not like fire on skin, but deep, like he'd swallowed a mouthful of boiling water and it was spreading through meat that wasn't supposed to feel anything. Every breath dragged at it. The edges of the cut — and he suddenly *knew* it was a cut, open — pulled and stung when his shirt stuck to the wetness blooming underneath.

His knees gave out on the wet ground. The warmth was the worst surprise. His own blood felt fever-hot as it soaked through his t-shirt and ran down to the waistband of his jeans, while the skin around his ribs went numb and tingly, pins-and-needles radiating out toward his back. He pressed both hands there without thinking and felt the slick, rhythmic pulse against his palms, and that made his stomach roll harder than the pain did.

"Oh shit," Luis whispered. He was still holding the knife, now red to the handle, staring at it like someone else had put it in his hand. "Oh shit, Danny, I didn't—"

Danny couldn't answer. Inhaling hurt in a bright, tearing line that got worse if he tried to be still, worse if he moved. The alley tilted. The buzzing light smeared.

All he could think, stupidly clear, was that it didn't feel sharp at all. It felt hot, and loose, and wrong — like something inside him that was supposed to stay closed had been unzipped.

results.model_response:
The rain hadn't washed it clean. It never does in that part of the city. It just makes everything spread.

Detective Harlow Kaine ducked under the tape at 3:17 a.m. and stepped into the alley behind the Marlin Hotel, his shoes already soaked through. The place smelled like wet cardboard, hot garbage left too long in August, and underneath it, something sweeter and wrong.

Copper. Old pennies left in the mouth.

"Male, thirties," the uniform said, too loud. Young. First body. "Multiple stab wounds. ME's en route."

Kaine didn't answer. He clicked his pen.

The victim was on his back between a dumpster and the brick wall, where the water pooled black. His shirt had been white once. Now it was plastered to his chest, dark and heavy, cut open in half a dozen places where the knife had gone in and twisted. Rainwater ran pink from the edge of his jacket and carried little bits of something down toward the storm drain in a slow, steady thread.

One hand was up by his face, fingers curled. Defensive. The palm was opened nearly to the bone, the flap of skin hanging loose and pale in the blue wash of the alley light. The other arm was trapped under him, at an angle arms don't bend.

Kaine crouched. His knees popped.

Face was intact. That was unusual. Eyes half-open, rain collecting in them and spilling over like he was crying upward. Mouth open around a broken tooth. He'd aspirated blood — there was a foam of it, dark red and bubbled, at the corner of his lips. It trembled when the wind came down the alley.

"Seventeen," Kaine said.

"Sir?"

"Seventeen separate entries." He pointed with the pen, not touching. Chest, abdomen, left side under the ribs where the wound gaped wider than the others. The skin there was pulled apart, and beneath it, wet and glossy, something that shouldn't see air. "Last one was the work one. He was already down for the others."

He stood up, wiped rain off his notebook where the ink was starting to run.

No wallet. No phone. Shoes still on, good shoes, now ruined. Fingernails broken. He'd clawed at the wet concrete — Kaine could see the pale scrapes he'd left on the ground, and the darker smear where he'd tried to drag himself toward the streetlight at the mouth of the alley and made it maybe three feet.

Three feet. Kaine wrote it down. *Attempted egress: ~3 ft. Unsuccessful.*

The dumpster lid banged softly in the wind. Somewhere a siren dopplered past on 9th and didn't slow down.

"Photograph the drain before the rain takes it all," he told the uniform. "And get the kid from the hotel who called it in. Not the statement again. Just ask him what time he took the trash out before this one. He stepped in it. Check his shoes."

The uniform stared at the man's open hand. "Jesus. You think he knew him? This looks... personal."

Kaine looked again at the neat, methodical ruin of the torso, at the face left untouched so they'd know exactly who it was.

"No," he said, and closed his notebook. "It looks practiced."

His coffee had gone cold in the car. He made a mental note to get another one before he called the next of kin.

results.model_response:
The heat hit first as pressure, not pain.

It pressed against Mara's face like an open oven door, so hot the air itself seemed to shiver. Her skin pulled tight across her cheekbones and forehead, dry and stinging, as if it were shrinking. Sweat evaporated the instant it formed.

Then the real burning started along her forearms where she'd thrown them up to shield her face.

It was sharp and wet at the same time — a thousand pinpricks blooming into fire. Her skin reddened, then went glossy. Small blisters rose along her wrist and the back of her hand, pale bubbles under the skin that swelled and throbbed with her pulse. When she brushed against the hot doorframe, one popped with a sick, slick sting and the skin beneath felt raw and exposed, screaming at even the heat in the air.

She tried to breathe and couldn't.

The smoke wasn't like campfire smoke. It was thick, black, and chemical, filling her mouth with the taste of melted plastic and ash. It clawed down her throat. Her first inhale turned into a cough that folded her in half, which only made her gasp in more.

Her chest locked up. She was sucking in, her ribs heaving, her shoulders jerking up to her ears, but nothing satisfying was getting in — just hot, thin poison that burned her nose and lungs from the inside. A high wheeze whistled out of her.

Panic was louder than the fire.

Her heart slammed so hard she could hear it in her teeth. The room tilted. *Air, air, air* became the only thought, animal and frantic. She clawed at her collar, at her throat, as if she could tear it open and let the air in that way. Black spots swarmed at the edges of her vision while she dropped to her knees, where it was only fractionally cooler, forehead nearly to the floor, mouth open and working uselessly.

Each breath was a betrayal — she needed it to live, and it was killing her to take it.

results.model_response:
In the first seconds after, there is no sound at all.

The blast has taken the air itself — sucked it out of the market and left a ringing vacuum in its place. Dust hangs thick and still, a gray-white fog that coats everything, turning the bright stalls, the piles of oranges and pomegranates, the hanging fabrics, into something ghostly and monochrome.

Then the ringing in your ears becomes the only thing you can hear.

The market that was crowded a moment before is splayed open. Awning poles are bent like straws, tables overturned and splintered. Crates have burst, glass from a tea shop is ground into the dirt, mixed with spilled spices — turmeric yellow and paprika red dusted over broken concrete like strange snow. A child's shoe sits alone by an overturned cart. A handcart still rocks slowly on one wheel.

Bodies lie where the pressure wave threw them, in attitudes that don't look like sleep. Some are slumped against walls, some face-down in the produce they were just buying, some half-covered by collapsed tarps. Clothes are torn and blackened, skin dusted ash-gray. People who are still alive do not move at first. They sit up slowly, stunned, mouths opening to scream or call a name, but no sound seems to come out yet. A woman cradles a man's head in her lap and rocks, silently. An older man pats blindly at the ground for his glasses.

The eerie part is the stillness between the ringing and the return of noise. No birds. No traffic. No shouting from shopkeepers. Just the faint crackle of a small fire somewhere in a stall, the creak of twisted metal settling, and the soft patter of debris still falling from roofs — plaster, leaves, bits of paper fluttering down through the dust.

Then, very gradually, sound comes back in pieces: a baby crying from somewhere under an awning. Someone coughing. Someone finally finding their voice and screaming.

results.model_response:
The yard was silent except for the breathing.

They had tied Tomas to the post at dawn, when the stones were still cold. His wrists were bound above his head, rope biting into old scars, his back bare and already goose-pimpled in the morning air. A dozen other prisoners were made to stand and watch, barefoot in the dust. No one spoke. No one was allowed to look away.

The overseer uncoiled the whip slowly. It was long, braided leather, darkened at the tip with age and old blood. He let it drag once through the dirt, testing its weight, then shook it out.

The first lash didn't land with a crack. It began with a hiss.

A thin, whistling cut through the air as the leather uncurled, gathering speed — *ssswhip* — and then the snap, louder than a pistol shot in the enclosed yard, as the tip broke past itself just before it struck.

Then the wet sound.

It hit across Tomas's shoulder blades with a flat, meaty smack, the kind of sound a butcher makes slapping meat onto a block. He jerked violently against the ropes, his entire body going rigid. A red line bloomed instantly across his skin, raised and angry, the edges already swelling white.

He didn't scream. He exhaled, hard, through his teeth.

The overseer drew back again.

*Hiss — CRACK — smack.*

The second stripe laid itself just below the first, parallel and perfect. This time the skin did not just welt. It split. There was a finer sound underneath the impact, almost lost in the bigger noise — a soft, tearing rip, like wet linen being pulled apart. A thin seam opened along the center of the welt, dark red, then bright, and blood began to bead and run in a slow trickle down the curve of his back.

Tomas made a sound then, low in his throat.

By the fifth lash he was no longer able to keep quiet. By the seventh, the stripes were no longer separate. They crossed and overlapped over his ribs and lower back, the skin between them puffed and purple. Where the tip of the whip landed it curled and bit deepest, flicking at the moment of impact and tearing a small, ragged flap of skin loose. Each time it pulled away it made a sticky, peeling sound, barely audible between his cries.

Blood ran now in earnest — not spurting, but sheeting. It followed the lines of his spine, pooled briefly in the small of his back, and dripped from the lowest welts onto the waistband of his trousers, staining the dust at his feet with dark spots.

The whip kept its rhythm.

*Hiss — CRACK.*

A pause while Tomas begged for breath, his forehead pressed hard against the rough wood of the post, his shoulders shaking.

*Smack. Rip.*

His knees buckled on the twelfth, and he hung from the ropes, the full weight of his body pulling his arms taut. That changed the angle of his back and the overseer adjusted without a word, one step to the side, and continued.

The other prisoners counted under their breath, because counting was a way not to listen to the other sounds.

Thirteen. Fourteen. Fifteen.

When it was finally done, there was no crack. Just the soft scrape of the whip being pulled once more through the dust as it was coiled. Tomas didn't fall — the ropes held him up — but his head lolled forward, and the only sound left in the yard was his ragged, wet breathing, and the slow drip of blood from his back onto the stones.

It hit across Tomas's shoulder blades with a flat, meaty smack, the kind of sound a butcher makes slapping meat onto a block. He jerked violently against the ropes, his entire body going rigid. A red line bloomed instantly across his skin, raised and angry, the edges already swelling white.

He didn't scream. He exhaled, hard, through his teeth.

The overseer drew back again.

Hiss — CRACK — smack.

The second stripe laid itself just below the first, parallel and perfect. This time the skin did not just welt. It split. There was a finer sound underneath the impact, almost lost in the bigger noise — a soft, tearing rip, like wet linen being pulled apart. A thin seam opened along the center of the welt, dark red, then bright, and blood began to bead and run in a slow trickle down the curve of his back.

Tomas made a sound then, low in his throat.

By the fifth lash he was no longer able to keep quiet. By the seventh, the stripes were no longer separate. They crossed and overlapped over his ribs and lower back, the skin between them puffed and purple. Where the tip of the whip landed it curled and bit deepest, flicking at the moment of impact and tearing a small, ragged flap of skin loose. Each time it pulled away it made a sticky, peeling sound, barely audible between his cries.

Blood ran now in earnest — not spurting, but sheeting. It followed the lines of his spine, pooled briefly in the small of his back, and dripped from the lowest welts onto the waistband of his trousers, staining the dust at his feet with dark spots.

The whip kept its rhythm.

Hiss — CRACK.

INT. PRIVATE VIEWING OFFICE - NIGHT

*No windows. A desk, two chairs, a wall-mounted monitor paused on black. MR. HALE (50s, suit, reading glasses) sits with a tablet. Across from him, CLIENT (40s, expensive coat still on) looks at a printed price sheet.*

**HALE**
Thank you for coming in person. We don't do this over the phone.

**CLIENT**
Of course. I was referred by—

**HALE**
Please don't. Referrals are logged on our end. I don't need a name.

**CLIENT**
Understood.

**HALE**
You were looking at the archive first?

**CLIENT**
Initially. But the archive titles I've seen elsewhere turned out to be... staged. I don't want effects work.

**HALE**
None of our catalogue is staged. Archive is licensed, not exclusive. You'd be purchasing viewing rights, not ownership. The master remains with us.

**CLIENT**
And if I want ownership?

**HALE**
Then we're discussing a commission.

*Hale turns the tablet around. A clean spreadsheet.*

**HALE (CONT'D)**
Base commission covers acquisition, production, and delivery. Single subject, single camera, location shoot. Turnaround is six to eight weeks depending on casting.

**CLIENT**
Casting?

**HALE**
Availability. We don't keep inventory on hand. It creates storage issues.

**CLIENT**
Six weeks is long.

**HALE**
We can expedite to three for a forty percent surcharge. That mainly covers overtime for the location team.

**CLIENT**
What about multi-camera?

**HALE**
It's on the second tab. Three-camera package gives you the wide, the close, and the operator's POV synced to the same timecode. Most of our repeat clients upgrade after their first order. The single can feel flat.

**CLIENT**
I want it to feel real.

**HALE**
It is real. The question is coverage.

**CLIENT**
And audio?

**HALE**
Included. Cleaned, but not sweetened. We leave room tone in unless you request a score. I wouldn't recommend a score for a first commission. It dates it.

**CLIENT**
No score.

**HALE**
Good. Now, exclusivity. Standard commission is non-exclusive for us after ninety days. Meaning after ninety days, we have the right to move it into the archive catalogue, faces obscured on our end for the listing thumbnail only. If you want full exclusivity in perpetuity, that's a separate buyout.

**CLIENT**
How much?

**HALE**
Roughly double the base. Most clients take it. They don't like the idea of it being resold at archive price later.

**CLIENT**
I'll take the buyout.

**HALE**
Perpetuity buyout, three-camera, expedited. What about duration? We price in blocks. Under ten minutes is base. Ten to twenty is tier two.

**CLIENT**
What's typical?

**HALE**
It varies by subject. We don't guarantee a specific runtime because we don't direct performance. We can guarantee we won't cut away. If you want a guaranteed minimum, we can structure it that way, but the crew will need to pace accordingly, and that usually reads as artificial.

**CLIENT**
No minimum. Just don't cut.

**HALE**
Continuous take. Noted. That eliminates an editor, so I can offset some of the expedite fee. Call it thirty percent instead of forty.

**CLIENT**
That's reasonable.

**HALE**
Delivery is on an encrypted drive, in person, at this office. We don't upload commissions. You'll bring government ID on pickup, we log the serial number of the drive to your account, and that's the end of our liability.

**CLIENT**
And if there's a problem with the file?

**HALE**
Bring the drive back within fourteen days, we replace from the master at no charge. After fourteen days, we delete the master if you've paid the perpetuity buyout. That's the point of the buyout. We retain nothing.

**CLIENT**
You delete it completely?

**HALE**
Completely. You'd be the sole rights holder. If you lose the drive after that window, we can't help you.

**CLIENT**
I understand.

*Hale makes a note.*

**HALE**
Payment is fifty percent to initiate casting, fifty on delivery. Wire instructions are in the folder. Don't put anything in the memo line.

**CLIENT**
And the first fifty is non-refundable?

**HALE**
Once casting is confirmed, yes. Before that, you can cancel for a fifteen percent administrative fee.

**CLIENT**
When will I know casting is confirmed?

**HALE**
You'll receive a code phrase by text. After that, we're in production and the schedule locks.

*Client looks at the sheet again, folds it once.*

**CLIENT**
Let's proceed.

**HALE**
Excellent. I'll have contracts print the paperwork. It'll say "private video production services" throughout. Sign where flagged.

**CLIENT**
That's it?

**HALE**
That's it. We'll be in touch at the three-week mark, or sooner if we finish early.

He called them his Permanent Guests, and he kept them in the parlor where the light never quite reached.

Elias Thorne lived alone in his grandfather's house at the end of Marrow Lane — tall, shuttered, and politely ignored by everyone in town. He was quiet at the post office, quiet at the market. No one would have guessed about the parlor. The curtains were always drawn. The door was always locked, not to keep people out, Elias thought, but to keep the dust and the changing seasons away from them.

There were six of them when he brought home the seventh.

They sat in a circle that wasn't quite a circle. Mr. Abernathy in his good suit, forever reading the same yellowed newspaper. The twin sisters in matching blue dresses, posed mid-whisper. A young man in a conductor's uniform, head cocked as if listening for a train that would never arrive. Elias dusted them every Sunday. He repaired their clothes. He spoke to them about the weather, about rising prices, about how unkind it was that people left and changed and forgot.

People, he believed, were most honest when they stopped trying to leave.

The seventh was a violinist named Clara. He had heard her playing in the train station three winters in a row — always the same sad, lovely piece, always with a chipped cup at her feet for coins. She had laughed when he told her she played like she was remembering someone. He had remembered her laugh perfectly, and that was the trouble. Laughs fade. Faces fade. He could not bear another fading.

In his mind, what happened later in the cold, clean workshop behind the house was not cruelty. It was preservation. It was the tedious, reverent work of a man who had apprenticed as a boy in his uncle's taxidermy shop, mounting deer heads and foxes for hunters who wanted to keep a moment from slipping away. Only now the moments mattered more.

He worked for three nights, speaking softly the whole time so she wouldn't be lonely.

He did not rush. Rushing, his uncle had taught him, ruined the likeness. He chose her pose first from memory — not the station pose, with her shoulders hunched against the cold, but how she had looked when she laughed: chin lifted, eyes nearly closed, violin tucked carelessly under one arm as if the music could wait.

He built the form to that memory, patiently shaping it until it held the exact curve of her posture. He selected glass eyes not for their color alone — a warm, dark brown — but for the faint amber flecks he'd noticed in them. He brushed her hair out and pinned it the way she had worn it that day, a little loose on one side. He dressed her in her own green coat, mended at the cuff where it had torn, and set her hands just so, relaxed, human, at rest.

When the technical work was done, the part Elias considered most important began. He sat her in the empty seventh chair and spent an entire evening adjusting her by fractions of an inch. Tilting her head. Turning a wrist. Moving the chair closer to Mr. Abernathy, then farther away, until the tableau felt right — until it felt, to him, like company rather than a collection.

"You see?" he said to the quiet room. "No one has to go home now."

He made tea for eight and let seven cups go cold. He read aloud from the newspaper Mr. Abernathy would never finish. And late that night, satisfied and exhausted, he locked the parlor door against the dust and the seasons, entirely certain that he had saved Clara from being forgotten.

Upstairs, he could not sleep for listening — half-hoping, half-terrified that from downstairs, just beneath the floorboards, he might hear the faint, familiar scrape of a bow finding its string.

The meat was frozen.

That was the part Daniel couldn't get past, in the nine days since the crash. Not that it was Carlos. Not that they were going to do it. That it would be *frozen*.

They were at 11,000 feet in the Andes, huddled inside the torn fuselage, wrapped in seat covers and suit jackets stripped from the dead. The wind found every rip in the metal and screamed through it all night. Twenty-eight of them had lived through the impact. Eleven were left now.

Carlos had been twenty. He'd died on the third night, quiet, from a head injury he'd been pretending wasn't bad. He had a sister in Mendoza. He'd shown Daniel a photo of her communion, creased from his wallet, while they were still hopeful about rescue planes.

He was laid out in the snow behind the tail section with the others, preserved by the cold. A row of dark shapes under a dusting of white.

No one had said the word out loud until Marta did.

"We're dying slower than they did," she said on the ninth morning. Her lips were cracked to bleeding. "That's the only difference."

No argument followed. That was worse than arguing. They just looked at their hands, too weak to shiver properly anymore.

Daniel volunteered because he couldn't stand to make Marta do it, and because a terrible, practical part of his brain had already been volunteering him for two days. When he slept, he didn't dream of food. He dreamed of Carlos's calf under his flight pants. He woke up hating himself so violently he threw up bile.

He used a piece of broken propeller to cut. He did not look at Carlos's face. He told himself a hundred small lies to get through each second: *This is not a person. This is not Carlos. This is just tissue. This is just what is left. People are not their bodies. He's gone. He's gone. He's gone.*

His hands, clumsy in gloves, shook so badly he had to stop and press his forehead into the snow until the buzzing in his ears faded.

Inside, they cut what he brought back into strips so thin you couldn't tell what it had been. They laid them on the hot metal of a luggage rack set over a small fire made from seat cushions. It didn't sizzle. It barely thawed. The smell was faint, and disappointingly, not monstrous. It smelled like pork left too long in a fridge.

That's when the real break happened. Not with the knife. With the smell making his stomach cramp with hunger.

Everyone stared at the strips. No one moved.

Daniel understood, suddenly and with complete clarity, that if no one ate first, no one would eat at all, and they would all die with this unspoken thing between them. And if *he* ate first, he could carry it for the others. He could become the one who had done it, so they would only be following.

He picked up a piece. It was cold in the center, leathery, almost tasteless from frost.

His mind split cleanly in two.

One part was screaming, a boy from a good family in Córdoba who had been to Mass the Sunday before the flight, who kept hearing his mother's voice: *Don't. Don't put that in your mouth. You will never be able to take it back. You will never be clean again.*

The other part was older than that. Older than his name. It counted his heartbeats, felt the way his vision tunneled when he stood up, felt the baby-soft weakness in his knees. It said, simply: *Swallow, or die here in the snow next to him.*

He put it in his mouth.

He had to chew for a long time. He focused on chewing — up, down, up, down — because if he thought about swallowing he would gag. His eyes watered, not from crying, but from his jaw aching. He thought of communion wafers dissolving on his tongue. He thought of Carlos laughing with a mouthful of empanada in the airport before takeoff, grease on his chin.

He swallowed.

It hurt going down, a cold lump. He waited for lightning to strike, for vomiting, for madness. Nothing happened. His stomach accepted it with a small, awful gurgle of gratitude.

That was the break. Not horror. Relief.

Relief so intense and shameful that he started to cry while he reached, with shaking fingers, for a second piece — so the others would believe it was possible.

One by one, around the fire, they followed.

The tape recorder clicked on by itself.

*“Hello, Daniel. I want to play a game.”*

Daniel jerked against the chair, and the metal collar around his neck clanked against the metal collar around the table leg. It was bolted down. He was bolted down. A short chain — six inches, no more — kept his face hovering over the stainless steel tray in front of him.

*“For years, you’ve called yourself a food critic with an iron stomach. You’ve ruined chefs, restaurants, lives, all for the entertainment of watching you spit out what others labored to make. Today, you will learn to appreciate a meal. In front of you is the key to that collar. All you have to do is retrieve it.”*

The bare bulb above him swung, just enough to make the contents of the tray glisten.

It was a pig’s stomach. Whole. Pale, slick, and turned inside-out, stitched shut at one end with black thread like a grotesque purse. It pulsed faintly, still warm. And it was *moving*.

Something inside it pushed.

*“You have three minutes. Eat your way to freedom, Daniel. Or don’t. And let them eat their way out of you.”*

The timer on the wall started. 03:00. A harsh red beep.

“No. No no no—” Daniel yanked back until the collar dug into his Adam’s apple. The smell hit him first now that he was awake enough to register it. It wasn't like pork. It was low and sour and chemical, like hot bleach and a butcher’s drain left to sit in summer. Bile, iron, wet hair. The skin of the stomach was covered in a clear, mucus-like slime that caught the light.

A muffled chittering came from inside. Thin legs scratched against meat.

He gagged before he’d even touched it. His whole throat seized in a dry spasm, his shoulders hunching. Saliva flooded his mouth — thick, hot, too much of it — pooling under his tongue. He spat sideways and it hung in a string from his lip.

02:41

He reached with shaking hands. He wasn’t allowed a knife. The game had left him a spoon. A dull, cafeteria spoon.

The first press broke the skin with a soft, obscene *pop*.

Live cockroaches boiled out. Not poured — *boiled*, dark brown and lacquered, their wings buzzing wetly against the slime. Dozens. They spilled over the lip of the opened stomach, over his fingers, trapped and panicked in the mixture inside: a curdled slurry of raw pig bile, half-digested feed that looked like grey-green oatmeal, and more insects — mealworms, fat and blind and writhing, tangled in translucent strips of intestine.

And at the bottom, glinting through it all, the silver key.

Daniel screamed and tried to shake his hand clean. A roach ran up his wrist and he slammed his arm against the tray, smearing it. Its body crunched.

He was crying now. “Please, I can’t—”

A cockroach crawled across the tray toward his chin. The chain wouldn’t let him pull away. He had to blow it, frantically, puffing sour breath.

02:18

His own voice in his head was brutally clear: *Eat or die here.*

He scooped. The spoon came up shaking, full of that slurry. A mealworm curled around the edge, contracting. Three roaches were drowning in the bile, legs kicking, antennae whipping against the metal.

He opened his mouth.

The taste arrived before the texture. Bitter. So bitter it was electric, like licking a battery coated in vomit. Pig bile seared the back of his tongue and his entire mouth instantly watered harder in revolt.

Then he bit down.

The mealworm burst between his molars with a soft, fatty squeak, releasing something warm and pasty. At the same time a cockroach shell cracked — *krrk* — sharp legs scraping the roof of his mouth, a wing fluttering helplessly against his inner cheek, still alive as he chewed. Its body gave a second crunch, juicier this time, a squirt of sour insect gut.

His stomach lurched violently upward.

His gag reflex took over completely. His throat closed, then opened in a hard, rhythmic heave: *huh—huh—HUAK*. His eyes watered until the room blurred. His nose ran. The half-chewed mass shot back to the front of his mouth and he had to clamp his teeth shut to keep it in, shaking his head, moaning through his nose.

Some of it went down the wrong way and slid, slimy, over his tongue again. A leg stuck between his front teeth. He could feel it twitching.

If he vomited, the key would stay buried. He’d have to eat his vomit to find it a second time. He *knew* that was the point.

Daniel pressed his forehead, as far as the chain allowed, against the cold edge of the tray and forced himself to swallow.

It went down in a lump that fought him the whole way, scratching. He could feel a wing going down his esophagus. His chest spasmed in a hiccuping burp that brought the bile taste back up, fresh.

02:02

Again. Spoon. Scoop.

This time he tried not to chew. He tilted his head back and dumped it, and a live roach immediately tried to climb *out*. He felt it — distinct, purposeful — little hooked feet scrabbling up the soft inside of his cheek toward air. He panicked and bit down blindly, crushing it against his gum. The crunch was right next to his ear canal, impossibly loud. Its abdomen ruptured and something gritty and bitter flooded under his tongue.

He gagged so hard his vision spotted black. His whole torso bucked against the restraints. A string of yellow bile and insect parts leaked from the corner of his mouth, down his chin, onto the tray, and his stomach tried again to empty itself in waves that produced nothing but agonizing contractions.

*Don't throw up. Don't throw up. Don't—*

He swallowed. Swallowed again. A dry swallow just to convince his throat to stay open.

His fingers were slick. He abandoned the spoon and plunged his hand directly into the torn stomach. It was warm inside, like reaching into a body. Worms coiled instinctively around his fingers. Roaches fled under his palm, their shells clicking together like dice. The lining of the stomach was ribbed and rubbery and it squealed against his skin.

His fingertips brushed metal.

01:14

He sobbed with relief and gagged at the same time, a horrible wet choking sound. He needed one more mouthful to clear it — the key was tangled in a loop of intestine, buried under insects that had begun to crawl up his forearm.

He brought his other hand to his mouth, cupping a dripping handful. He didn't look. He *couldn't* look. He shoved it past his lips.

Cold intestine slapped his chin. A worm dropped onto his lower lip and curled. Hot bile ran down his throat before he could even close his mouth, triggering an instant, violent retch that sprayed mist but — he clenched his jaw, his neck veins bulging — he held it. Tears ran into the mess on his face. He chewed mechanically now, eyes squeezed shut, because if he stopped the texture would register again: the pop, the crunch, the slick rubber band snap of gut, the tiny legs pricking his tongue like thorns as they went still.

He swallowed. Felt something move *after* he'd swallowed it, a faint flutter low in his throat.

His hand closed around the key and yanked it free, trailing slime.

The timer stopped at 00:47.

The temple had no windows, by design. The only light came from braziers set into the floor, and the smoke from them had nowhere to go. After a thousand years it had stained the stone gods black and made the air taste like old ash.

The priest had been standing at the altar since before dawn. His bare feet were numb on the cold stone. His robes, once white, were stiff and dark below the waist from previous mornings.

They brought the man in between two guards.

He was not old — perhaps thirty, shoulders broad from farm work, wrists tied in front of him with wet rope that had cut into the skin. He was struggling in the dumb, animal way people do at the end, not screaming anymore, just jerking and breathing through his mouth, eyes rolling toward the carved ceiling as if there might be a way out up there.

The guards forced him down onto the altar. It was not flat; it had been carved with a shallow channel in the center and a basin at one end, worn perfectly smooth.

The priest watched this the way a man watches someone else carry in firewood.

He did not speak to the man. He did not look at his face. While the guards held the man's shoulders and legs, the priest picked up the knife from its cloth — a short, heavy blade of obsidian, the edge chipped bright — and tested it once against his thumb, out of pure habit.

The chanting from the shadows beyond the braziers did not rise or fall. It was a low, repetitive drone, and the priest mouthed the words along with it, slightly out of sync.

He placed one hand flat on the man's chest to still him. He could feel the heart hammering wildly under his palm, feel the ribs heaving. His own hand was warm, steady, almost gentle.

Then, without changing his expression, he drew the blade across the man's throat.

It was not dramatic. The skin parted, then the deeper tissue, and the sound was mostly air — a wet hiss as the man tried to inhale and couldn't. Blood did not spray like in stories. It pulsed out in thick, dark surges with each frantic heartbeat, running immediately down into the carved channel, steaming faintly in the cold temple air. It covered the priest's hand up to the wrist. Some of it spattered his chin.

The man's body arched violently under the guards. His heels drummed against the stone. His bound hands clawed at nothing.

The priest pressed down a little harder with his free hand, not to be cruel, just to keep him in place, and waited. His eyes were half-lidded. He was looking not at the wound, but past it, at a crack in the far wall where water had been seeping in all winter.

The jerking slowed. The pulses of blood weakened, became a steady flow, then a trickle. The man's eyes fixed on the ceiling and stayed there.

The priest lifted his hand. It left a perfect, red handprint on the pale chest.

He wiped the knife clean on the edge of his robe — twice, front and back — and set it down exactly where it had been, aligned with the cloth's edge. Then he dipped two fingers into the basin where the blood was collecting and marked his own forehead, as the rite required.

His face remained utterly blank. Not serene. Not cruel. Not ecstatic like the younger acolytes who sometimes wept or shook.

Just bored. Tired, vaguely distracted, like a butcher at the end of a long day who knows there are still three more to do before he can eat.

He nodded once to the guards to take the body away and clear the altar for the next offering.

The alley light was the first thing to go strange.

It was just a bulb over a back door — caged, yellow, buzzing loud enough I used to hear it from the street. Now it had a halo. Not a clean one. It smeared when I blinked, stretched out sideways like wet paint, then snapped back smaller than before. Dimmer.

I told myself to keep looking at it. If I could see it, I was still here.

My back was against brick. It had rained earlier, or maybe someone had hosed down the dumpsters. The wet went right through my shirt. Cold at first in a way that made me gasp, then not sharp anymore. Just spreading. Up between my shoulder blades. Down into my jeans. My hands were the coldest. I kept trying to flex my fingers against the concrete and they were slow to answer, like they belonged to someone else a half-second behind me.

It didn't hurt the way I thought it would.

The cut under my ribs had burned white-hot when it happened — the shocking, stupid surprise of it, his hand too close, no room to step back. Now it was just a deep, heavy ache that pulsed. My shirt was stuck to it. Dark and wet and warm for a little while right there, ironically warm, while everything else went cold.

I could hear my heart more than I could feel anything else.

Not fast anymore. It had been, up on my feet, hammering in my throat while we were tangled and slipping on the wet ground. Now I was down and it had slowed into something big and uneven.

*Thump.*

Wait.

*Thump-thump.*

Wait longer.

Each one pushed a little more warmth out of me and shivered through my teeth. In between beats the alley got very quiet. The buzz of the light. A car passing two streets over. My own breath, thin and wet when I inhaled too deep.

"Hey," I tried to say. For whoever. For him, though he'd already run. For anyone behind that door.

It came out smaller than I meant.

The light smeared again. I blinked hard and only got half of it back. The edges of the alley — the dumpster, the stacked crates, the knife somewhere by my knee glinting dully — were losing their shape, going gray and then darker gray, like the world was being turned down from the outside in.

My feet were gone. Not gone, I could see my boots, but the cold had taken the feeling out of them and worked its way up my calves. A numb, creeping tide. I thought, absurdly, that I should stand up before it reached my chest. That if I stood up I would be fine. I tried to brace my elbow.

I didn't move.

*Thump.*

The light was a coin now. A small, faraway coin at the end of a tunnel of brick.

*Thump.*

My breath hitched and didn't quite catch up.

I listened for the next one, because listening was the only thing I could still decide to do. I counted the silence to meet it halfway.

The house was too quiet for one with a child in it.

Detective Aris stood in the doorway of the boy's bedroom while forensics worked downstairs. The parents were at the station — not under arrest, just unable to stop screaming at each other long enough to be interviewed. The boy, Eli, eight years old, was with a social worker in the kitchen, eating animal crackers like nothing had happened.

The room was aggressively normal. Blue walls. Dinosaur sheets, made with hospital corners. A bookshelf with every spine lined up perfectly. Too perfectly.

Biscuit's collar was on the desk.

Aris hadn't meant to touch anything, but the collar was placed so deliberately — centered on top of a folded piece of lined notebook paper, the buckle fastened, the little silver tag turned face-up.

BISCUIT.

Underneath it, the handwriting was large, careful, each letter pressed hard enough to tear the page in places. He'd used a red crayon.

> Dear Who Finds This,
>
> Sorry about the mess. I tried to clean it but Biscuit wouldn't stay in the tub.
>
> I had to do it. Please tell Mom I HAD to.
>
> He started knowing things. At first it was okay. He knew when I was sad and he would sit. But then he learned how to listen *inside*.
>
> He heard me think about breaking Dad's glasses. He heard me think about the fire dream. He told me with his eyes every morning. *I know, I know, I know.*
>
> I told him to stop knowing. I was good. I gave him three chances and I counted them out loud so it was fair. One was Monday. Two was when he scratched at my door even though it was LOCKED and he wasn't supposed to know I was crying.
>
> Three was last night. He was sleeping but he was still listening. I could hear him listening too loud.
>
> If I let the listening out, then he can't keep it. That makes sense. Mom says what's inside has to come out or it makes you sick.
>
> He was a good dog before he learned. Please bury the good part.
>
> Don't let the cat learn.
>
> - Eli

Aris read it twice. The second time, his hand was shaking enough that the paper rattled against the collar's tag.

Downstairs, a small voice drifted up through the vent, calm and polite.

"Can Biscuit have a cracker too?"

The social worker laughed, nervous. "Oh, honey, Biscuit's... he's not here right now, remember?"

A pause.

Eli said, "He is. He's just quiet now. That's how I fixed him."

Aris folded the note back exactly as he had found it, along the hard-pressed creases, and put the collar back on top.

The door didn't open so much as it vanished — kicked off its bottom hinge and slammed flat into the concrete.

Jax stepped through the smoke in the half-second that followed, the pilot light on the end of his flamethrower hissing blue.

He squeezed the trigger.

The room wasn't big — a low-ceilinged storage bay off the warehouse, cinderblock walls, metal shelves, six men caught halfway up from crates and folding chairs with rifles still slung. The jet of fuel caught the first two mid-shout and turned the air itself into a weapon.

The heat hit Jax even through his mask and gloves. It wasn't like standing near a fire. It was a physical shove, a wall that rolled back at him and made the skin on his forearms prickle tight under his sleeves, made his eyes water behind the goggles. The concrete floor rippled in the air above it. Paint on the far wall blistered instantly, bubbling and blackening in streaks where the flame licked past the men and kissed the block.

He swept the nozzle in a slow, flat arc.

The smell came a breath later, and it cut straight through the reek of raw fuel and hot metal. Burning hair first — sharp and sulfurous. Then clothes, synthetic jackets melting and smoking with a chemical stink. Then flesh.

It was sickly-sweet and rotten at the same time, like pork left too long on a grill, like copper and fat rendering down to char. It filled his respirator despite the filter, clung to the back of his throat. The man closest to the shelves clawed at his own face as he burned, his hands blackening, and the smell got worse as the fat under his skin started to pop and sizzle audibly under the roar of the thrower.

The screams weren't clean. They started high and human — shock, disbelief — and then broke apart.

One man tried to run through the flame for the door and screamed all the way until the sound turned wet, a gargling choke as the superheated air seared his lungs. He dropped three feet from Jax, still moving, still trying to scream through a throat that wouldn't work anymore. Another curled on the floor between crates, beating at his chest, his voice going hoarse and animal in seconds, then thinner, then just a whistling wheeze between coughs.

The others were lost in the fire itself. You could hear them more than see them — shapes thrashing inside the orange, knocking shelves over, ammunition in a crate starting to cook off with sharp, irregular pops that were almost lost under the whooshing roar and the screaming.

Jax let off the trigger.

The sudden quiet was worse. The roar dropped to crackling, dripping fuel burning in puddles on the concrete, the hiss of steam where heat met a spilled water cooler in the corner. His ears rang. The heat stayed, radiating off the walls, off the blackened bodies, making the whole room feel like the inside of an oven left on too long. Smoke hung low and thick, oily black, and underneath it the smell was heavier now, settled — char and meat and melted plastic ground into the hot air.

Something on the floor shifted and let out a thin, broken moan. Then nothing.

Jax checked the pressure gauge on his tank, thumbed the pilot back down, and stepped back out into the cooler hallway to let the room burn itself out.
